claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires processing above 2300 °C.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 has relatively high porosity and residual microstructural defects.
Porosity and residual defects in conventional ZrB2 contribute to damage during liquid plating-bath exposure.
A liquid-phase precursor route can provide homogeneous nanoscale diboride powders.
Applying the liquid-phase precursor route to pure ZrB2 will achieve molecular-level reactant mixing.
Liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 powder can be densified by spark plasma sintering at approximately 1800 °C.
Spark plasma sintering is a faster processing route than the alternative technique discussed in the cited high-entropy oxide study.
Combining nanoscale precursor-derived powder with SPS will produce a refined and homogeneously distributed microstructure in single-phase ZrB2.
The refined microstructure will minimize pore formation and enhance grain-boundary bonding during ZrB2 densification.
Molecular-scale mixing lowers the activation energy for ZrB2 densification.
Rapid heating and short dwell time during SPS will produce fully sintered, dense single-phase ZrB2 at approximately 1800 °C.
Lower-temperature precursor/SPS processing will reduce holes and other defects that permit liquid ingress during plating-bath exposure.
Precursor/SPS-processed ZrB2 will be denser and less porous than conventionally sintered ZrB2 processed above 2300 °C.
Precursor/SPS-processed ZrB2 will have mechanical strength comparable to or greater than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Precursor/SPS-processed ZrB2 will show fewer microstructural weaknesses than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Precursor/SPS-processed ZrB2 will resist hole formation and degradation during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
The proposed preparation boundary lowers the nominal sintering temperature from above 2300 °C to approximately 1800 °C.
The proposed comparison measures density, porosity, mechanical strength, microstructure, hole formation, and mass loss before and after controlled long-duration plating-bath exposure.

Prior evidence from analogous high-entropy diboride and oxide systems supports precursor synthesis of ultrafine powders and rapid SPS processing, but does not establish long-term plating-bath integrity for pure ZrB2.
